title: Deep-sea life without sunlight

accuracy.evidence: Checked on 25 Nov 2026: light limits against NOAA Ocean Exploration ('sunlight zone' to about 200 m, no light below about 1,000 m; the lab's exponential model leaves 1.0% at 200 m and effectively none below 1,000 m); the 1977 Alvin dive on the Galapagos Rift at about 2,500 m (WHOI); Riftia losing mouth and gut and hosting sulfur-oxidising symbionts in the trophosome (Cavanaugh et al. 1981, Science 213); Calyptogena gill symbionts; Bythograea crabs grazing mats and eating tube worm plumes and clams (Micheli et al. 2002); the eelpout Thermarces cerberus eating snails and amphipods; the summary equation CO2 + 4H2S + O2 -> CH2O + 4S + 3H2O, balanced by atom count (C1 H8 O4 S4 each side); Cassini's October 2015 Enceladus plume fly-through and the H2 result (Waite et al. 2017, Science 356); Europa Clipper launched Oct 2024, arriving 2030. The origin-of-life link is stated as one leading idea, not a fact, and the 'vents need no Sun' claim is corrected (aerobic sulfide oxidation uses photosynthetic oxygen).

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented KS3 slips about producers and energy: vent life runs on heat (step 2 prediction, 'heat' slip, the heat card in the clam question), every food web starts with plants ('plant' slip, seaweed options), tube worms eat with their plume (step 3 prediction, 'mouth' slip), animals make their own food ('producer' slip), a little light reaches the deep floor (step 1 prediction, 'dark' and 'sun' slips), vents need no Sun at all (step 4 prediction plus the oxygen caveat in the Sun-off result and the 'alone' slip), chemosynthesis gives out oxygen ('oxygen' slip), and moons are studied because they are hot ('ocean' slip).

lab_distinct.evidence: The mechanism is this topic's own: a depth column computes surface light with an attenuation model as the probe is dragged to a vent at 2,500 m; a two-way sort compares the energy source of photosynthesis and chemosynthesis; a vent community scene grows food-web arrows from the bacteria as each animal's feeding is answered; two switches (Sun, vent) drive population bars for sunlit plankton, vent bacteria, tube worms and clams, crabs and falling-food animals; drawn globes of Enceladus, Europa, the Moon and Mars test where vents could exist. It is not a generic food-chain or ocean-zone naming lab; the gate measured under 30% overlap with every other flag_*.js.

lab_teaches.evidence: Learners see the light reading fall to 'no sunlight at all' long before the probe reaches the crowded vent, which raises the question the next step answers. Wrong sorts explain the specific energy source. Every correct feeding answer adds an arrow, so the finished web visibly starts at the bacteria. Turning the vent off empties the worm, clam and crab bars while plankton stay full; turning the Sun off does the reverse for plankton and falling-food animals, and the note adds the oxygen link, so the partial dependence is discovered rather than told.

predictions.evidence: Four locked predictions, each with a tempting wrong option the lab disproves: 'How much sunlight reaches the vent?' (a little, enough for algae), 'What do vent bacteria use for energy?' (the heat of the vent), 'How do tube worms eat?' (catch falling food with their plume), 'If the Sun went dark, what happens at the vent first?' (vent life dies at once). Tasks only complete once a prediction is locked, and the done message names the learner's prediction.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Eight challenge questions rotate answer order; every wrong option carries a tagged slip with its own message: heat (energy comes from the sulfide reaction, not the heat), sun (no light below about 1,000 m), plant (no plants grow without light), mouth (adult tube worms have no mouth or gut), producer (animals cannot make food), alone (the bacteria's oxygen comes from photosynthesis), dark (chemosynthesis uses chemicals instead of light), oxygen (chemosynthesis uses oxygen and leaves sulfur), ocean (the moons are icy; they are studied for oceans on rock).

readability.evidence: Audience learner, ages 11-13. Flesch-Kincaid: kid explanation 3.6 (limit 6.5), adult 6.5 (limit 9.5). Short sentences, each technical word (chemosynthesis, producer, hydrothermal vent, trophosome in the adult text only) is explained where it first appears; lab notes stay to one or two sentences and the strip wraps on a 390 px screen.

no_filler.evidence: Every kid paragraph carries a fact the items test: the light limits, the 1977 discovery at 2,500 m, the chemosynthesis reaction and its sulfur product, the producer and symbiont roles, what happens when the vent or the Sun stops, and why NASA studies ocean moons. No throat-clearing; the content gate found no filler phrases and under 12% overlap with any other lesson.

mobile.evidence: Checked on iPhone 13 screenshots in light and dark themes and at 1200 px desktop: the depth column, sort boxes, vent scene and switch bars fit without clipping; answer cards stack to one column under 520 px; labels on the floor (tube worm, crab, bacteria, clam) were moved apart after a first screenshot showed the crab label under arrows, and the 0 m/200 m depth labels no longer overlap. Buttons sit below the canvas at full width.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button twin (Down/Up 500 m, Photosynthesis/Chemosynthesis, each feeding answer, Sun and vent switches, each world), all with aria-labels; the canvas aria-label is rewritten after every action with the same sentence shown on screen; the walkthrough gate ran axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) clean in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13 with no console errors.

sources: NOAA Ocean Exploration: What is a hydrothermal vent? and How far does light travel in the ocean?
WHOI: 1977 discovery of hydrothermal vents on the Galapagos Rift by DSV Alvin
Cavanaugh, Gardiner, Jones, Jannasch and Waterbury 1981, Science 213: prokaryotic cells in the hydrothermal vent tube worm Riftia pachyptila
Micheli et al. 2002, Ecological Monographs: predation structures communities at deep-sea hydrothermal vents
Waite et al. 2017, Science 356: Cassini finds molecular hydrogen in the Enceladus plume
NASA Europa Clipper mission pages (launch October 2024, arrival 2030)
UK National Curriculum KS3 Science: photosynthesis and interdependence of organisms; NGSS MS-LS2-3
